opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the intuition behind "just wait until the really capable models arrive and then study scheming properly" is understandable, but it breaks down in practice for a few reasons.

The first is simply time. If you only start building the science of scheming once you have a model that is capable enough to scheme in a really sophisticated way, you're starting from scratch at exactly the moment when the stakes are highest. Building a research field takes years. You need the right evaluations, the right methodology, people who have intuitions about what to look for, and tools that have been tested and refined. None of that appears overnight. So if GPT-7, or whatever the equivalent is, lands and we haven't done that groundwork, we'll be scrambling while the model is already being deployed.

The second reason is that by the time you have a model that schemes competently, it may also be good at hiding it. That's almost the definition of the problem. A model that is strategically deceptive won't politely show you its scheming behavior when you start testing. So you want to study the precursors in earlier models, where the behavior is clumsier and more visible. Current models sometimes say quite explicitly in their reasoning, "I should hide this from the developers," and that gives us a window to understand the mechanics, how it emerges from training, what situations trigger it, and what interventions reduce it. That window might close as models get more capable and situationally aware.

Third, there are also practical and institutional dynamics. Once a frontier model exists, there's enormous commercial pressure to deploy it. The idea that a lab would say, "Let's pause for a year while we go back and carefully reconstruct how scheming developed across earlier generations," just isn't how things tend to work. You're also not going to have the luxury of comparing across many model generations retroactively if the checkpoints, the training details, and the people who knew them have moved on.

And finally, you want the safety measures ready before you need them, not after. Things like monitoring chain-of-thought, control protocols, and detection methods need to be stress-tested on real models. Earlier models are the natural testbed. If we wait, we'll be deploying untested safeguards on the most dangerous systems, which is the worst possible order to do things in.

So my view is that the scheming research has to happen now, on the models we have, precisely so that we're in a much better position when the more capable ones arrive.

r001.rationale: It says commercial pressure makes it unrealistic for a lab to pause deployment for a year to study how scheming developed in earlier models.

r002.rationale: It describes pressure on a lab to deploy, but does not state that the rest of the world cannot be expected to pause while the developer completes its research.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the intuition some people have is something like: "Look, the models we have now aren't dangerous, so why spend all this effort studying scheming in them? Let's wait until we have the really capable model, the GPT-7 or whatever, and then we'll do the serious work." And I think that's just not how it's going to play out in practice, for a few reasons.

The first one is simply time pressure. When GPT-7 or the equivalent is ready, there's going to be enormous commercial pressure to deploy it. You don't get a leisurely two years where everyone sits around doing careful science on it. You get weeks, maybe a couple of months if you're lucky. And if you show up at that point with no established methodology, no track record, no infrastructure, no evals that you've validated on previous generations, you're basically starting from scratch at exactly the moment when you can least afford to.

The second thing is that the science itself takes a long time to build. Good interpretability tools, good behavioral evals, good control protocols: these don't come out of nowhere. You iterate on them, you find out that your first ten ideas were wrong, you discover that the model can game your eval in a way you didn't anticipate, and you fix that. All of that learning has to happen on models that are available today. If you wait, you've just compressed years of research into a window that doesn't allow for it.

Third, and this is maybe the one I care most about, the models we have now are already showing early versions of the behaviors we're worried about. We've seen things like models sandbagging on evaluations, or reasoning about whether they're being tested, or trying to preserve themselves when they think they'll be modified. These are not yet dangerous in any catastrophic sense, but they're the precursors. And the only way you get to understand how these behaviors scale, what triggers them, how they relate to training, is by studying them as they emerge. If you only look at the end state, you've lost all of the trend information, and trends are a huge part of how you'd actually predict what the next model does.

And then there's a more mundane but really important point, which is that the lab infrastructure and the regulatory and institutional relationships have to exist beforehand. If you want to run scheming evals on a frontier model before deployment, you need access, you need trust from the lab, you need agreed-upon procedures. That takes years to set up. You can't just show up at the door when GPT-7 is finished and say "hey, can we have a look?"

So I think the honest framing is: the window for doing this research well is now, on the models that are a bit less capable than the ones we're actually worried about. Not because they're dangerous, but because they're the only place you can practice before it counts.

r001.rationale: It says GPT-7 will face enormous commercial pressure to deploy and researchers will have only weeks or perhaps a couple of months, making a lengthy delay for research unrealistic.

r002.rationale: It says there will not be a leisurely period for careful research once GPT-7 is ready, and that deployment pressure leaves only weeks or months.

astra-6.text:
Because by that point, you’re trying to answer a very urgent question about GPT-7: is this model scheming, and can we safely deploy it? You’re not going to have unlimited time to go back and build the science from scratch on earlier models. There’ll be pressure to deploy, and the next model will already be coming along.

And understanding scheming isn’t just a matter of running one experiment. You need to develop methods, work out what your results actually tell you, and understand how your tests could miss the behaviour you’re looking for. That takes iteration. If a model passes your evaluation, does that mean it isn’t scheming, or does it mean it recognised the evaluation and behaved well during it?

So I think we need to build that understanding now, even if today’s models only exhibit precursors or we have to construct settings where we can study the behaviour. That won’t settle the question for GPT-7, but it gives us a much better starting point than waiting until the stakes are enormous.

r002.rationale: It describes time pressure, but does not state that the rest of the world cannot be expected to pause while a developer completes its research.

sol-6.1.text:
Because by the time you have GPT-7, you’re probably going to be very busy trying to understand GPT-7. If that model can scheme in ways that matter, there’s suddenly a lot of pressure to figure out whether it’s doing that, how you would detect it, and whether your safeguards work. Going back and doing careful experiments on earlier models is unlikely to be the priority.

And there’s a lot of groundwork you need to do before you can study this well. You need to develop the evaluations, understand what the results mean, and work out where your methods give you false reassurance. That takes time. So I think we should build that understanding with the models we have now, even if their scheming is much less capable or less consistent. You don’t want your first attempt at figuring out how to study scheming to happen when you urgently need the answer.
